terms.grammar: often with populī; to hold one, concursum facere
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.4.52: quem concursum in oppidō factum putātis?
terms.comment: A running together of people, and so an uproar, a tumult (Lewis & Short); Morgan–Owens gives populī concursus for a public protest, and Egger concursum facere for demonstrating. It also means a clash, a collision.

terms.gloss: the plebs’ walk-out: Rome’s mass protest
terms.comment: The people of Rome left the city in a body until their demands were met; sēcessiō alone is a withdrawal, a secession (Lewis & Short).
Traupman’s word; in late Latin a declaration (Symmachus, the Vulgate; Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: quem concursum in oppidō factum putātis, quem clāmōrem, quem porrō flētum mulierum?
phrases.english: what a gathering of people do you think there was in the town, what shouting, and what weeping of women besides?

sources: Lewis & Short: concursus · Lewis & Short: secessio · Lewis & Short: protestatio
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. demonstration, public protest.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 302, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).
